messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling R package preprint
messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk,

I wanted to alert you to a preprint from folks at St Andrews and NOAA
about the R package "Distance" (available on CRAN):

Distance Sampling in R

David Lawrence Miller, Eric Rexstad, Len Thomas, Laura Marshall, Jeffrey
Laake

Estimating the abundance and spatial distribution of animal and plant
populations is essential for conservation and management. We introduce
the R package Distance that implements distance sampling methods to
estimate abundance. We describe how users can obtain estimates of
abundance (and density) using the package as well documenting the links
it provides with other more specialized R packages. We also demonstrate
how Distance provides a migration pathway from previous software,
thereby allowing us to deliver cutting-edge methods to the users more
quickly.

http://biorxiv.org/content/early/2016/07/14/063891

We hope this is useful!

cheers,
--dave

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Too much binning?
messages.body_plain:
You cannot use AIC to select cutpoints.  AIC values can only be compared when models are fitted to the same data, and by binning the data in different ways, they are not the same.

You have rounding to 50m, so you need to choose cutpoints that avoid 50m – i.e. choose cutpoints so that any distance recorded as 50m is probably in the correct distance interval.  E.g. if you have a lot of rounding to the nearest 10m (but not to the nearest 5), you might select interval cutpoints of 0, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, …

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Wanted: Collaborators for distance sampling animal movement project
messages.subject_clean: Wanted: Collaborators for distance sampling animal movement project
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance-sampling listers:

Animal movement a problem in your distance sampling survey?  Want to be on the cutting edge of solving it??  Read on!

Richard Glennie, a PhD student at CREEM, is working on methods to incorporate movement modelling into distance sampling, and he is looking for suitable data to illustrate the application of this model.  Details of the project and the data requirements are given below.  If you have such data and are interested in colloborating with Richard, then please let me know (len.t...@st-andrews.ac.uk) and I'll put you in touch with him.

PROJECT DETAILS

When surveyed animals move fast relative to the observer, distance sampling methods can overestimate abundance. Richard's model accounts for the animal movement, reducing this
overestimation.

The model requires two data sets: distance sampling survey data and movement data.

The distance sampling survey data must include for each detection the location (either in (x,y) coordinates or (radius, bearing) form) and the time of detection.  We also need the time each transect was started, the path taken and the speed (average speed over the whole transect is OK -- or time at waypoints along the transect).

Movement data will usually come from a sample of tagged animals.  These do not need to be collected on the same animal population that the distance sampling survey was conducted. We require only that the tagged animals move similarly to those that were surveyed. Observations collected at a small time-scale would be desirable as it is movement over the short time it takes to survey a transect that is important.

Thanks folks! Len

messages.body_plain:
Steve

Without looking at your data, I suspect the main challenge to producing precise estimates of abundance is your small number of transects.  You have but three transects, whereas general guidance is to have something on the order of 15-20.

Variability in your abundance estimate is a combination of uncertainty in your detection function and uncertainty in encounter rate.  The main contributor to uncertainty in line transect estimates is encounter rate variance.  With only three transects you have a very poor estimate of that encounter rate variability.  All of the explorations you describe in your second paragraph may reduce some uncertainty in your detection function, but that uncertainty is usually small relative to the uncertainty in encounter rate.

Improving precision in your estimate will likely only result from an improved design in your survey with greater emphasis placed upon estimating encounter rate variability; via increased numbers of transects.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalia, hi listfolk,

I think the easiest way to think about this is to treat the detection
function fitting and spatial model separately.

The detection function could be fitted either way (subtracting 200m or
by left truncation), though I think that left truncation is more
consistent (perhaps over folks here disagree with me). It also seems
nicer to do this at the modelling stage, rather than editing your data.

The segment length is what you need to give to dsm in the "Effort"
column of your segment data. dsm will calculate the correct segment
areas by multiplying the truncation distance (right truncation minus
left truncation) by 2 (to get both sides of the plane) and then
multiplying that by the segment length. This will ensure that you have
the correct area for each segment. You didn't survey in the blind spot,
as you couldn't see anything there, so that should not be included in
the survey effort.

To obtain environmental covariates from e.g., GIS, one often needs to
take some summary of values inside the segments (mean, median, standard
deviation etc). In that case it's easier to not include the blind spot
in your polygons. I doubt that it makes any difference in most cases
whether you have the "full" segment or one with the hole down the middle
-- we're generally interested in broad-scale effects, not minutia. This
can be done using e.g., the ArcGIS toolbox MGET provided by folks at Duke.

Hope this helps!

All the best,
--dave

Alejandro

In my opinion, if you have flight height information for each sighting, you might as well use it.

I understand your comment about lots of heights would maps several distance bands into potentially many band midpoints.  However, I wonder if that is true in practice.

If the number of bands you have is small (such that they are each quite wide), and the fluctuations in altitude is reasonably small, there may actually not be much reward from recomputing band interval midpoints for each detection.

I've not conducted a distance sampling survey from the air, so I might be talking rubbish, but it would seem a similar discussion about fluctuations in band locations, could be had for changes in aircraft roll; I suspect few if any practitioners attempt to correct for roll.

(Ramble soon coming to an end) I suspect that unless the altitude changes are extreme, there may be little impact upon the survey estimates resulting from such altitude adjustments.  I'm happy to be proved wrong.

I expect Eric is right.  However, it's easy to test if you use R because the function ddf (distance detection function) in the mrds package allows for binned data with a different bin location for each observation.   Instead of a distance column in the input dataframe, you have bistbeg and distend.  In the meta.data function argument, which takes a list, you set binned=TRUE, and you can specify a different left and right truncation for each observation (which is also going to be a result of varying altitude) by passing in a matrix of left and right truncation points to int.range.  Have a look at the help for the ddf function for details.  This facility is only available for single platform models (method="ds") -- if anyone has a double-platform aerial survey where different bin width per observation would be helpful please let us know.

Cheers, Len

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Error in t(partial) %*% vcov : non-conformable arguments
messages.body_plain:
Hello listers,

Dave managed to work out a fix for this problem in the package. He told me that the issue is that when estimating so many parameters and with binned data, the Hessian (or rather the covariance matrix) for the detection function gets hard to estimate. In this case the failure to estimate the covariance matrix means that the abundance estimation procedure also fails.

The fix can be downloaded by following the instructions here : https://github.com/distancedevelopment/distance/#getting-distance

He also mentioned that when working with binned data it is best if less factors be used since binned data loses some of the information that the raw data would contain.

Hope this helps you all in the future
>
